title: 【从零开始的Godot游戏开发】#08 敌人刷新与战斗闭环
text:
Alright, welcome back to 'Godot Game Dev from Scratch.'
At this point,
there's just one last piece of the puzzle left to complete
for our game's core gameplay system.
In this video,
we'll finish up the enemy spawning
and player damage mechanics.
As for the smaller stuff like sound effects and UI,
we'll save that for the next video to wrap things up.
First, let's head over to the Game scene,
create a new Node two D, and name it EnemyContainer.
This node isn't responsible for display or runtime logic;
it just acts as a container.
Later on, all the enemies we spawn
will be attached as child nodes under this node,
which prevents them from being scattered
directly under the root '
'game' node.
Later on, if we want to count or manage all the enemy objects,
we just need to iterate through the child nodes
of this 'EnemyContainer' node.
Just a little trick.
Then, let's create another Node two D,
and call it 'EnemySpawnPoints'.
This node is also a container of sorts,
where we'll attach the enemy spawn points.
What node marks the spawn points? We'll add a child node
and search for 'Marker two D'.
The description below also makes it clear:
Marker two D is a generic two D position hint for editing.
After double clicking to add it,
drag it out from the map's origin
point to the spawn entrance on the left,
then rename it to 'SpawnLeft'.
Next, add another Marker two D, name it SpawnRight,
and drag it to the right side of the map.
Then, add one more, SpawnBottom, placing it at the very bottom.
These three nodes only mark locations,
and aren't involved in collisions or other logic.
Marker two D is ideal for spawn points,
target points, path points,
or camera reference points—any auxiliary object
that just needs a position.
So, some of you might be asking, if all I need is a position,
can't I just use a Node two D?
Of course, you can!
Like we always say,
game development is flexible—especially in Godot,
you can use various node approaches for the same function.
The engine itself provides this semantic best practice.
So, using Marker two D
is just so much clearer than Node two D,
right?
Then, let's add a Timer node and name it EnemySpawnTimer.
The timer will control the spawning rhythm, signals, and logic,
all managed in the script later.
Then, let's drag the 'WorldBounds' node—
which defines the map boundaries—
and place it at the end of the list.
This isn't a necessary step and doesn't affect game logic;
it's just my personal habit.
Grouping nodes that
are closely related to the scene's logic together
makes things look a bit clearer.
Alright, let's start coding.
Right click the Game root node,
select 'Add Script,'
keep defaults, and create.
But before we dive into writing code,
let's first sort out our design approach
for the monster spawning logic.
In our final project,
the goal of the game is to survive until the countdown ends.
The game's difficulty will ramp up over time,
without distinct waves;
enemies will continuously spawn randomly
from designated points.
Enemy stats don't change,
but their spawn frequency increases,
forcing players to face more enemies.
So, we can use linear interpolation
to control the spawn interval
and achieve this escalating difficulty.
First, let's write some code
to set up our enemy spawning resources.
The enemy scene is the body, the configuration the soul –
a data driven approach to resource setup is key.
Next, we'll define some variables
related to the spawn rhythm.
Their meanings are clear in the comments.
This 'initial_spawn_count' variable
controls the number of enemies that spawn
right at the start of the game—not just to make it easy
for us to test
if the spawning function is working properly.
It's also a small design touch
to get players into the action quickly, without waiting.
Finally, these last two variables
limit the minimum spawn interval
and the maximum number of enemies
that can exist on the field at once.
This habit of thinking about controlling boundary conditions
is something I hope you'll gradually develop
as you follow along with our tutorial.
If we keep linearly increasing the spawn frequency,
then when a developer extends the level's duration,
In the late game,
a ton of enemies might spawn on the map all at once,
which would be totally impossible to handle.
So, we've set up some limits here
to prevent these extreme situations from happening.
Now, let's write the node references and variables.
For the node reference code,
you can get it by holding Ctrl and dragging the node,
but make sure the naming is consistent with ours
to make copying it over easier.
The names and comments below are self explanatory.
We've done some caching.
At the start,
we scan and cache the scene tree and config resources
to avoid frequent rescans during updates,
improving performance.
Then, we implement `_ready` and `_process`. In `_ready`,
we sequentially call our wrapped functions.
scan the spawn points and configuration resources
and download them.
then initialized the spawn timer
and the first batch of enemies.
The process update function is simple:
we increment the game time
and then call `_update_spawn_interval`.
This function, highlighted in red,
is one we haven't implemented yet.
Don't worry, we'll get to the code
for each of these right away.
First, let's implement these two functions
for our 'collect' download.
The get_children method
allows you to get a list of all nodes
attached beneath a specific node in the Godot node tree.
We find the nodes of type Marker two D
and put them into the 'enemy_spawn_points' download array.
Caching enemy configuration resources
simply involves checking their validity
and ensuring the configuration isn't empty.
Next up is the function for configuring the enemy
spawn timer;
we'll set it to trigger repeatedly.
Set the calculated timer duration,
then connect the signal in code for its trigger logic.
Next up is the implementation of the `_update_spawn_interval
l` function,
which dynamically calculates the timer interval
based on the current game time.
This is one of the core pieces of code
for our difficulty scaling.
Here, we're setting the current spawn interval,
not handling the spawning logic itself.
And there's a small detail here.
When the difficulty ramps up,
the old timer might still be waiting for a long time.
By calling 'start',
we can switch the current round to a faster pace,
making the difficulty change more responsive.
Now, for the `_get_current_spawn_interval` function,
which is the other half of our spawn rate control,
this is where we calculate the current spawn interval.
Start interval is the initial spawn interval, with 'maxf'
ensuring it's no less than zero point one.
End interval is the late game minimum.
This ensures it's no less than zero point one,
and not exceeding the start interval.
If spawn_acceleration_duration is less than or equal to zero,
we'll just return the final time interval
and then calculate the difficulty ratio.
We use clampf to keep it between zero and one,
then use the lerp function to perform linear interpolation.
Now, this logic might sound a bit abstract,
so let's try to picture it like this.
In the game, the enemy spawn frequency—that is,
the difficulty—constantly ramps up,
which is controlled by the spawn interval.
At the start of the game,
the spawn interval is one point five seconds;
by the end of the game, it's zero point six seconds.
So, as the game progresses,
the enemy spawn interval will gradually decrease
from one point five down to zero point six
in a linear fashion.
So moving on, we defined these two functions:
spawn_initial_enemies...
It immediately spawns enemies at the start
by calling _try_spawn_enemy
a specified number of times in a for loop.
` _start_enemy_spawn_timer
r` starts the enemy spawning timer.
We first check if the Enemy Spawning System is ready,
then start the timer.
Then, for the enemy spawn timer, once the time is up,
the logic is to make a looping call—calling
the _try_spawn_enemy
function as many times as needed
for a single spawn wave.
Now, at this point, many of you might have realized
that we've hidden and encapsulated
the actual enemy spawning logic
inside the _try_spawn_enemy function.
This makes calling it from the higher level code
clean and convenient.
You just call it, and an enemy appears.
How do we implement it?
The logic is quite simple.
First, we run some preliminary checks
to see if the Enemy Spawning System is ready
and if the number of enemies on the field
has reached its maximum.
Then, we randomly pick a spawn point,
randomly select an enemy type,
instantiate the enemy scene,
attach it to our container node,
and set its proper spawn position.
Then, using the setup method,
we assign the randomly selected configuration
to bring it to life.
Then, we'll provide three short functions:
is_spawn_system_ready,
which checks if the Enemy Spawning System is up
and running properly.
whether the player exists,
if the enemy scene is present,
and if the spawn points
and enemy configuration resources are empty.
As for `_pick_spawn_point`,
the core idea is to use the randi_range function
to get a random index within a range,
then randomly pick one from the enemy spawn points
and return it.
` pick_enemy_config` is similar,
randomly picking one from enemy config resources.
Then there's the get_alive_enemy_count function,
which basically just counts the number of enemy type
child nodes
under the Enemy_container.
Some might ask, doesn't get_children return an Array?
Why not just use its size?
Because items from dead enemies
could be under that parent too.
So, to be precise, when we count the enemies on the field,
we'll only count the ones that are still alive,
not the ones that are already 'boxed'.
Of course, when you're encapsulating similar features,
make sure to get into this good habit,
because nodes and the scene tree are very flexible.
Anything could be dynamically added or removed.
So the best way is to check the type
to see if it's the node we're looking for.
Oh, there's an error here—let's click on it and jump over,
and it turns out to be spawn_acceleration_duration.
We missed defining this variable.
We can head to the top of our code and add this definition.
This variable is just for testing purposes in this video,
to complete the logic loop
for the entire enemy spawning module.
Then, in the next video when we cover UI progress,
we'll switch to a different code implementation.
Once that's done, we can't start testing just yet,
because there's still some logic
we need to add to the player script.
Let's switch over to the player script. First,
at the end of the constants at the top,
add the definition for 'blink_enabled'—our player character
will also have a flashing effect
when taking damage.
So, this whole setup uses the same logic
we already implemented
for items and enemies—making them flash
via a shader material.
Then, scroll down, find where the @export variables are defined,
and add these three variables:
the player's movement speed,
maximum health, and the duration of the brief invincibility
flash after taking damage.
Then, add these three runtime variables:
current health, remaining invincibility time,
and whether the player is currently dead.
The ones exposed with @export up top
are basically pre game Settings,
while these variables keep track of things during runtime.
Next, scroll down to the `_ready ` function,
delete it entirely, and replace it with this code.
Basically, it just initializes the current health value
we just defined,
and then sets up the properties for the hurt flash effect.
We'll implement the red highlighted function later.
Now, moving down to the `_physics_process
` function—let's just replace the whole thing for clarity.
The key parts here are the logic at the top
for updating invincibility
time, checking for death, and stopping movement.
Next, we'll add the `apply_damage` function here,
as the player's unified damage entry point.
If the player is dead, or the damage value is less than zero,
or the player is still in their invincibility period,
return false.
If damage can be successfully dealt,
we decrement current_health;
if health hits zero, we call `_die`;
if not dead yet, we activate a short invincibility period.
So yeah, that's pretty simple too.
Next, we also added a get_current_health function
to query the player's current health externally.
We won't be using it in this video, though.
We'll use this later for the UI to display player status.
It's short,
so let's just put it here for now.
Then, let's add the logic here
to update the player's invincibility time.
Basically, it decrements the remaining invincibility time
based on the passed in frame interval,
and if that time runs out, it turns off the flashing effect.
Then, we add functions to activate invincibility
and manage the flashing.
When the player's health hits zero,
it enters a death state,
though without a dedicated death animation.
So when the player dies, all we do is halt the logic,
which works in tandem with the logic
in our earlier `_physics_process
` function to stop the player from moving and shooting.
and then turn off the Funnel enhancement animation.
Now that the code is written,
set the shader material for our player's animation node,
then switch to the player scene tree and repeat.
Click on the BodySprite node,
go to 'Material' on the right and select 'New ShaderMaterial',
then use 'Quick Load' to pick our 'blink' shader.
Since we only have one player character,
it's fine to leave this unchecked.
Alright, so now that we've pretty much hooked up
all the systems,
it's time for a test.
Let's run the current project—
we can see the enemy spawning is working fine,
and we've already tested the shooting function,
which is also okay.
But once the enemy dies, a bug pops up.
The enemy's death animation
just keeps looping in place and never disappears.
Plus, the death animation is playing a bit too slowly.
This bizarre effect happens
because we failed to disable looping
for the death and explosion animations,
so the animation finished signal won't trigger.
In the bottom left File System,
under the animation folder,
double click on each enemy's animation resource one by one.
In the editor panel that opens,
click this small button
to turn off looping for the death animation,
and then change its playback speed from five to ten FPS.
Also, ensure the Exploding Enemy's 'explode' animation
is non looping,
and apply the same settings to all other enemies.
So now, if we run the test again,
we can see that enemy spawning and dying
are both working properly.
But we noticed something.
When the player shoots near the map edge,
bullets can penetrate our invisible boundary wall
and fly outside.
We run into the same issue when shooting at obstacles.
When the player's gun barrel is right up against an obstacle,
the bullet won't be blocked by it.
But wait, didn't we already implement collision for bullets
with obstacles and the Invisible Wall?
So why is this still happening?
Let's turn on 'Show Collision Shapes' in the debug menu
and run it again to get a clearer look.
When we were handling the bullet firing,
to make the visuals a bit better,
The bullet is offset from the player's position,
firing roughly from near the muzzle
of the player's animation.
So, when the player is against the map boundary
or an obstacle and fires a bullet,
the bullet spawns outside the map or inside an obstacle,
which makes our previous bullet to terrain
collision handling ineffective.
Actually, in the previous chapter
where we covered the shooting implementation,
some of you sharp eyed viewers
might have already spotted this issue.
Using this bug as cover to shoot from—now
THAT's a creative idea, haha!
But here, just to be absolutely thorough
and leave no stone unturned,
I want to walk you through
how we can completely prevent
this bullet clipping through issue from occurring.
Let's start in the Bullet script, at the constant definitions.
Here, we've added this line,
which is identical to the code
we wrote earlier in the bullet script,
to define what the physics layer for our world collision is.
This 'one' is the first binary layer.
Then, head over to the `_try_shoot ` function,
remove the `has_spawned_bullet` check, fire the bullet directly,
and reset the shoot timer
to see if the bullet can be fired successfully.
We'll handle this within the call
chain of the fire_blaze function.
Next, let's head over to the spawn_bullet function
and add these two lines of code right at the start:
We use `_can_spawn_bullet` to check if a bullet can be spawned.
If not, we simply return false,
and stop any further bullet instantiation from happening.
So, right below that,
we can provide the implementation
for the can_spawn_bullet function.
Actually, it's almost the same logic
we used to prevent bullets
from passing through the Invisible Wall.
Using a two D ray,
we perform a check before the bullet spawns
to see if there are any obstacles
between the player's center
and the bullet's position.
If there is, it means the player's gun muzzle
might have gone into an obstacle
or outside the world bounds.
We can directly check
if the raycast's 'hit_result' dictionary is empty
to get a boolean value for whether a collision occurred.
Besides that, for the spiral shooting function below,
we don't need all that hassle anymore.
We can just remove this 'i' check and fire the bullet directly.
Now, running the game again. Shooting near walls,
bullets won't clip through.
And at the world's edge, they won't fly off.
And with that,
all the core combat logic for our game is now complete.
This video features many scattered changes
to the player.gd script,
so to help you quickly check and fix issues,
I've put all the code for the player script
so far right here
for you to cross reference and check against.
In the next video,
we'll wrap up the final parts of the project
by integrating the game's UI and sound effects.
and then I'll show you
how to package and publish our very first game,
covering the entire process from start to finish.
Thanks for your Triple Combo and enthusiastic sponsorship!
I'm Voidmatrix, and I'll see you in the next video!

# Enemy Spawning and Combat System Overview

## 总览
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    GS["Game Scene"] --> EC["EnemyContainer (Node2D)"]
    GS --> ESP["EnemySpawnPoints (Node2D)"]
    ESP --> MLeft["SpawnLeft (Marker2D)"]
    ESP --> MRight["SpawnRight (Marker2D)"]
    ESP --> MBottom["SpawnBottom (Marker2D)"]
    GS --> EST["EnemySpawnTimer (Timer)"]
    GS --> PB["Player (Node2D)"]
    PB --> BScript["Bullet Script"]
    GS --> WB["WorldBounds (Node2D)"]
    PB --> UI["UI (future)"]
    EST --> ES["Enemy Spawning Logic"]
    ES --> EC
    ES --> ESP
    PB --> PD["Player Damage Logic"]
    PD --> EC
```

## 敌人生成流程
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Ready["_ready()"] --> ScanPoints["scan_spawn_points()"]
    Ready --> CacheConfig["cache_enemy_configs()"]
    Ready --> InitTimer["init_spawn_timer()"]
    InitTimer --> StartTimer["_start_enemy_spawn_timer()"]
    StartTimer --> TimerTimeout["Timer timeout signal"]
    TimerTimeout --> TrySpawn["_try_spawn_enemy()"]
    TrySpawn --> CheckReady["is_spawn_system_ready()"]
    TrySpawn --> CheckCount["get_alive_enemy_count() < max_enemies"]
    TrySpawn --> PickPoint["_pick_spawn_point()"]
    TrySpawn --> PickConfig["pick_enemy_config()"]
    TrySpawn --> Inst["instance enemy scene"]
    Inst --> AddToContainer["add_child to EnemyContainer"]
    AddToContainer --> SetPos["set spawn position"]
    SetPos --> Setup["apply enemy configuration"]
```

## 难度随时间线性递增
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Process["_process(delta)"] --> IncTime["increment game_time"]
    IncTime --> UpdateInterval["_update_spawn_interval()"]
    UpdateInterval --> GetInterval["_get_current_spawn_interval()"]
    GetInterval --> Lerp["lerp(start_interval, end_interval, ratio)"]
    Lerp --> Clamp["clampf(ratio, 0, 1)"]
    GetInterval --> CheckDuration["if spawn_acceleration_duration <= 0"]
    CheckDuration --> ReturnFinal["return end_interval"]
    Lerp --> SetTimer["EnemySpawnTimer.wait_time = calculated_interval"]
    SetTimer --> RestartTimer["EnemySpawnTimer.start()"]
```

## 玩家受伤与无敌闪烁
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    ApplyDamage["apply_damage(damage)"] --> Guard["if dead or damage<0 or invincibility>0 → return false"]
    Guard --> Decrement["current_health -= damage"]
    Decrement --> DieCheck["if current_health <= 0"]
    DieCheck --> Die["_die()"]
    DieCheck --> Invincibility["activate_invincibility()"]
    Invincibility --> Flash["start_flash_effect()"]
    Flash --> UpdateInv["_physics_process(delta) updates invincibility timer"]
    UpdateInv --> EndInv["if timer <= 0 → stop_flash_effect()"]
    ApplyDamage --> GetHealth["get_current_health()"]
```

## 子弹生成与墙体碰撞防止
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    TryShoot["_try_shoot()"] --> RemoveCheck["remove has_spawned_bullet check"]
    RemoveCheck --> ResetTimer["reset shoot timer"]
    ResetTimer --> SpawnBullet["spawn_bullet()"]
    SpawnBullet --> CanSpawn["_can_spawn_bullet()"]
    CanSpawn --> RayCheck["2D raycast from player_center to bullet_spawn_pos"]
    RayCheck --> Collision["if hit_result not empty → return false"]
    Collision --> NoSpawn["abort bullet creation"]
    RayCheck --> NoCollision["proceed"]
    NoCollision --> Instantiate["instance bullet scene"]
    Instantiate --> AddBullet["add_child to scene"]
    AddBullet --> SetPos["set bullet position"]
    SetPos --> SetVelocity["apply initial velocity"]
```

```mermaid
    DieCheck --> Die["_die()"]
    DieCheck --> Invincibility["activate_invincibility()"]
    Invincibility --> Flash["start_flash_effect()"]
    Flash --> UpdateInv["_physics_process(delta) updates invincibility timer"]
    UpdateInv --> EndInv["if timer <= 0 → stop_flash_effect()"]
    ApplyDamage --> GetHealth["get_current_health()"]
```

## 子弹生成与墙体碰撞防止
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    TryShoot["_try_shoot()"] --> RemoveCheck["remove has_spawned_bullet check"]
    RemoveCheck --> ResetTimer["reset shoot timer"]
    ResetTimer --> SpawnBullet["spawn_bullet()"]
    SpawnBullet --> CanSpawn["_can_spawn_bullet()"]
    CanSpawn --> RayCheck["2D raycast from player_center to bullet_spawn_pos"]
    RayCheck --> Collision["if hit_result not empty → return false"]
    Collision --> NoSpawn["abort bullet creation"]
    RayCheck --> NoCollision["proceed"]
    NoCollision --> Instantiate["instance bullet scene"]
    Instantiate --> AddBullet["add_child to scene"]
    AddBullet --> SetPos["set bullet position"]
    SetPos --> SetVelocity["apply initial velocity"]
```
